Impacts of Productive Safety Net Program on Rural Household’s Asset Accumulation in Kutaber District, Ethiopia

Esmael Eshetu Feleke

This is a preprint; it has not been peer reviewed by a journal.

https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9716594/v1

This work is licensed under a CC BY 4.0 License

Abstract

The Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP) in Ethiopia aims to address food insecurity, foster productive investments, and promote rural economic growth and environmental rehabilitation. While many studies have evaluated the general impacts of the program, there is limited empirical evidence on its specific outcomes, such as asset accumulation, particularly at the local level. This study assesses the PSNP's contribution to asset accumulation by examining the experiences of 138 participants and 152 non-participants across two kebeles using both primary and secondary data. The study focused on three outcome variables: tropical livestock units (TLU), productive assets, and non-productive assets. Descriptive and inferential statistics were used to analyze socio-economic and demographic factors. Due to the absence of baseline data, propensity score matching was applied to compare participant and non-participant households. The econometric results revealed that PSNP participation was positively influenced by dependency ratio (in AE) and landholding size at a 5% significance level. However, factors such as education level, frequency of extension contact, TLU, off-farm income, and distance to market negatively affected participation, also at the 5% probability level. The findings indicate that the PSNP had a negative impact on both TLU and non-livestock asset accumulation. Beneficiaries primarily utilized transfers for consumption rather than for saving or investment activities, reducing the program’s contribution to asset building. The study concludes that program designers, implementers, and funding agencies need to re-evaluate the PSNP to enhance its effectiveness in promoting household asset accumulation and achieving its broader objectives.
